newsitem.title: POLAND: POLAND MULLS CONVERTIBLE BONDS TO FUND REFORM.
newsitem.headline: POLAND MULLS CONVERTIBLE BONDS TO FUND REFORM.

text.p: The Polish government may issue convertible bonds exchangable for shares of privatised firms to finance the crucial reform of the country's social security system, officials preparing the reform said on Wednesday.

The five to seven-year bonds, likely to be sold at a discount, could be issued in 1999 or even next year if parliament passes several crucial bills triggering the reform in 1997, a treasury ministry adviser Krzysztof Pater said.
"The bonds would be available both to domestic and foreign investors," Pater, member of the team of experts preparing the pension system reform, told a news conference.

But many politicians, including Labour Minister Tadeusz Zielinski, has said party bickering before this year's parliamentary elections is likely to delay the passage of the reform plan well beyond this year.
Pater said that under his team's proposal the bonds would be exchangable for shares in a group of about 70-80 companies with best financial results, which still remain state-owned.
Pater said that under the latest proposal the bonds could be exchanged a stek of up to 80-percent in a firm undergoing privatisation.
The government has earlier said only 30-percent stakes in such companies would be used in the social security system reform.
